summary: Epoch semantics and isExpiredAt are properly constrained -- takenOverBy +2, takenOverBy +0, renewedUntil bumping the epoch, isExpiredAt '>' instead of '>=', and isExpiredAt returning a constant were all applied to Lease.java, run, and all KILLED. The two flagged tests: replacing the byte-identical check with the exact byte sequence was the right fix and genuinely discriminates (an encode field-order swap is killed; returning that test's own expected constant is killed by the other two encode tests, which use different value sets -- they are not redundant, they cover each other's blind spot). The empty-endpoint test's technique is legitimate TDD, but the assertion it settled on constrains nothing beyond 'no throw' and leaves the exact lease shape M4 writes in production silently corruptible on read. The parser is where the tests stop constraining: four behaviour-changing mutations survive the full suite, and the unescapable-value path corrupts a lease with no test anywhere. All mutations reverted; git diff clean; staged hash still 766d7fae.

findings.title: aMalformedOrTruncatedLeaseIsRefused constrains none of decode's three shape guards -- three behaviour-changing mutations survive the whole suite
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED, three separate mutations of Lease.java, each with :format:test --tests binjava.format.LeaseTest green. (1) Delete `|| s.charAt(s.length() - 1) != '}'` from Lease.java:209 -- a lease truncated by exactly ONE byte then decodes as a fully valid Lease[epoch=1, holderPodId=pod1, holderEndpoint=e, expiresAtMillis=5]. The test truncates by THREE bytes (line 136-137), which removes `:5}` and so exits through the non-numeric expiresAtMillis path instead of the brace path -- the brace guard is executed but never constrained, and a one-byte truncation is the likeliest short read. (2) Delete `s.charAt(0) != '{' || ` from Lease.java:209 -- `"epoch":1,...}` with no leading brace decodes fine; the `not json` case at line 134 fails the TRAILING brace check too, so it never isolates the leading one. (3) Delete the `if (at < 0) throw` guard from stringField (Lease.java:222-224) -- `{"epoch":1,"holderEndpoint":"e","expiresAtMillis":5}` with holderPodId absent decodes to Lease[holderPodId=lderEndpoint, ...], i.e. a FABRICATED holder for the object that decides who may write the commit chain. No test in the suite decodes an object missing a string field at all: the only missing-field input is `{}` (line 132), which exits through longField(epoch) before stringField is ever reached. Fix: truncate by one byte; strip the leading brace; and omit each of the four fields in turn. Asserting on hasMessageContaining would also separate the paths.

findings.title: The empty holderEndpoint -- the only endpoint value M4 ever writes -- is never put through the codec, so the exact production lease shape can corrupt on read with the suite green
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED. Mutate stringField at Lease.java:226 from `int end = s.indexOf('"', from)` to `s.indexOf('"', from + 1)` -- a one-character off-by-one that breaks ONLY the empty-string case. Full suite green. Then `new Lease(0, "pod1", "", 1000L)` encodes to `{"epoch":0,"holderPodId":"pod1","holderEndpoint":"","expiresAtMillis":1000}` and decodes back to holderEndpoint=`",` -- round-trip equality false, silently. That is precisely the lease M4 writes, since the row states holderEndpoint is EMPTY in M4. On the direct question asked: writing a deliberately over-strict skeleton to red an 'X is allowed' test is legitimate under testing.md rule 2 and I do not fault the technique. The defect is the assertion it settled on -- `assertThat(l.holderEndpoint()).isEmpty()` (line 151) is true by construction for a record accessor, so the red proved only the skeleton's own strictness and nothing about the code that shipped. The one-line fix that makes the red real: `assertThat(Lease.decode(l.encode())).isEqualTo(l)`, which kills the mutation above.

findings.title: decode throws unchecked IllegalArgumentException for a well-formed lease with an invalid value, and no test covers decode on that path
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the unmutated code: `Lease.decode("{\"epoch\":-1,\"holderPodId\":\"p\",\"holderEndpoint\":\"\",\"expiresAtMillis\":5}")` throws IllegalArgumentException, not IOException, from a method declared `throws IOException` whose javadoc (Lease.java:203-205) says it 'REFUSES anything that is not exactly this shape, loudly and now'. Same for a negative expiresAtMillis and for a blank holderPodId. The three validation tests (aNegativeEpochIsRefused:59, aBlankHolderPodIdIsRefused:69, aNegativeExpiryIsRefused:78) exercise the CONSTRUCTOR only -- and aNegativeEpochIsRefused's own comment names 'corruption or a hand edit' as the source, which is the decode path it does not test. aMalformedOrTruncatedLeaseIsRefused covers shape but never a value. M4.3b's LeaseManager will wrap decode in `catch (IOException)` per the SPI convention and this escapes it, so a hand-edited or corrupted lease surfaces as an unchecked exception instead of the refusal the format promises. Whether decode should map it to IOException is the production reviewer's call; the test gap is that decode's value-validation failure path has no test at all. Add a decode case per invalid value and pin the exception type.

findings.title: encode cannot escape and decode cannot unescape, nothing refuses the characters that break the codec, and no test covers it in either direction
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the unmutated code, all three silent -- no exception, no failing test. (a) `new Lease(1, "p\",\"holderEndpoint\":\"HIJACKED", "real:9200", 5L)` encodes to a document that decodes to holderEndpoint=HIJACKED; round-trip equals() is FALSE. That is the field M5's commit forwarding uses to REACH the holder, per the row's own justification for shipping it now. (b) `new Lease(1, "a\"b", "e", 5L)` round-trips to holderPodId=`a` -- silently truncated. (c) `new Lease(1, "a\nb", "e", 5L)` emits a raw newline inside a JSON string, which is not valid JSON, so `jq` rejects it -- defeating the 'legible with cat' justification the entire hand-rolled codec rests on. The javadoc at Lease.java:125 asserts 'a podId refuses - and / upstream'; that guard lives in CommitRequest in the sequencer module, does not run here, and would not refuse `"` if it did. aLeaseRoundTripsThroughItsEncoding uses only benign values ('pod1', '10.0.0.4:8080'). So there is no test proving refusal upstream and no test pinning the behaviour here: the reviewer's question 'refused upstream or silent corruption path' resolves to silent corruption. Either the compact constructor refuses the characters the codec cannot represent -- with a test covering `"`, `\\`, newline -- or a test must document the corruption explicitly. Under non-negotiable 8 this is a wire format, so fixing it later is a format change.

findings.title: The non-numeric guard in longField is an equivalent mutant and its comment overstates its role
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: replacing `if (end == from)` with `if (false)` leaves the full suite green, and correctly so -- Long.parseLong("") throws NumberFormatException, which the catch at Lease.java:253 maps to the same IOException. The guard is redundant, so the badNumber case at LeaseTest:140 is killed by the catch, not by the guard. Recording it so nobody later writes a test 'for' that branch and believes it constrains something: the nine-line comment credits the guard with refusing a quoted number when parseLong is what actually does. No test change needed; if the branch is kept for its distinct message, assert the message.

findings.title: decode's leniency -- reordered fields, duplicate fields, unknown extra fields -- is entirely unpinned in either direction
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the unmutated code: `{"expiresAtMillis":5,"holderEndpoint":"e","holderPodId":"p","epoch":1}` decodes fine (order-independent); `{"epoch":1,"epoch":9,...}` decodes with epoch=1 (first wins); `{...,"checkpoint":"x"}` decodes ignoring the extra field. No test asserts any of these is intended, and no test refuses any of them, so `decode` could be made strict or lenient in either direction without a failure. Two of the three matter here: duplicate-field-first-wins is the exact mechanism the escaping finding exploits, and 'an unknown field is ignored' is a forward-compatibility decision on a CAS'd object that the M4.3 row explicitly forbids pre-adopting a checkpoint field into -- which is a decision worth one test either way.

findings.title: 'All 11 mutation verified' reads stronger than what was measured
findings.failure_scenario: The row's closing claim is defensible under the reading 'each of the 11 tests was verified to kill at least one mutation', and I believe that reading is true. But it will be read as 'the covered code is mutation-clean', and it is not: four behaviour-changing mutations of Lease.java survive the whole suite (findings 1 and 2 above), three of them in the decode path the row does not mention. testing.md rule 9 sets the floor at 80% killed on changed code, so a bare 'mutation verified' invites the stronger reading. Suggest stating what was verified -- per-test red records against named mutations -- rather than a global claim. The row is otherwise honest and unusually detailed about both weak-test episodes, including that the byte-identical check passed against a stub returning '{}'.

verified_clean: Epoch semantics, all KILLED as applied mutations with the suite run: takenOverBy advancing by 2; takenOverBy not advancing; renewedUntil bumping the epoch. LeaseTest:112-122 and :99-108 constrain every component of both derived leases.

isExpiredAt: '>' instead of '>=' KILLED; `return false` KILLED. LeaseTest:85-95 pins 999/1000/1001, so the inclusive boundary is genuinely nailed. The signature takes the instant as a parameter -- non-negotiable 7 satisfied, and it is the right shape for M4.12's simulation.

Parser field lookup: swapping which field stringField reads (holderPodId <-> holderEndpoint) KILLED by the round-trip test's distinct values; swapping longField epoch <-> expiresAtMillis KILLED. Deleting the `s.length() < 2` guard KILLED (empty input then throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, not IOException).

theEncodingIsExactlyThisByteSequenceIncludingFieldOrder is the right replacement and discriminates: swapping the holderPodId and holderEndpoint clauses inside encode is KILLED. And it is not redundant with theEncodingIsReadableJsonAnOperatorCanInterpret -- an encode that returns the exact-bytes test's own expected constant is KILLED by the other two encode tests because all three use different value sets. Good judgement on both counts.
Tier: T0 throughout. No clock, socket, store, Thread.sleep, fixed port or system temp. testing.md rules 1, 15, 16, 17 satisfied.

Independence: every test builds its own values, no shared mutable state, no ordering dependence. Names describe behaviour (rule 12). Plain @Test, so neither M0.17 composed-annotation blind spot nor the JVM-crash blind spot applies.
No existing assertion weakened -- both source files are new.
